title: Marilyn Hotchkiss Ballroom Dancing & Charm School
full_review:
If, by chance, the title "Marilyn Hotchkiss Ballroom Dancing & Charm School" (Samuel Goldwyn) sounds vaguely familiar, it's because it was used by filmmaker Randall Miller for his well-received short film of 15 years ago. That one concerned a 12-year-old boy who attends a cotillion and discovers that girls "aren't so bad."

Using the short as a springboard, Miller has come up with a feature film with a nonlinear story line about emotionally scarred widower Frank Keane (Robert Carlyle with his trademark hangdog expression), who works for a bakery. His wife apparently took her own life.

His life changes when he comes across a terrible car wreck while making a delivery. The mortally injured driver, Steve (John Goodman), is pinned in the front seat, and as Frank talks to him to keep him conscious, Steve relates how he was en route to a reunion (planned 40 years earlier) with Lisa, his grammar-school sweetheart. They had arranged to meet on the fifth day of the fifth week of the fifth month of the new millennium. (Steve and Lisa were the characters in the short.)

The appointed place was the dance class of the title where the two children enjoyed their puppy love. (There are numerous flashback scenes, which use footage from the short film.)

At the request of the dying man, Frank dutifully goes to the dance where he's welcomed by emotionally fragile instructor Marienne (Mary Steenburgen), daughter of the school's founder, and the ladies of the group, including Sonia Braga and pretty Meredith (Marisa Tomei), though he's eyed with suspicion by the latter's hotheaded stepbrother, Randall (Donnie Wahlberg), who values his position as the class's alpha male. (Meredith harbors a poignant secret: She has a prosthetic leg, a result of childhood abuse at the hands of her stepfather.)

Eventually, Frank brings his bereavement group mates (Sean Astin, Ernie Hudson, David Paymer, Miguel Sandoval, David St. James and Adam Arkin) to the class, where they all, presumably, find healing.

Director and co-writer Miller's compassionate film (written with wife Jody Savin) has several touching bits and is well acted by its name cast, including Danny DeVito and Camryn Manheim. The original Steve (Elden Henson) has a cameo here too and, it goes without saying, looks far more like his younger self than Goodman.

But a jagged pace, often-stilted dialogue and monochromatic color palette make the film ultimately more dreary than uplifting.

Those British films that deal with ordinary folks who open themselves up to life and find purpose (for example, "The Full Monty," "On a Clear Day" and "Kinky Boots") strike a much more satisfying balance between the dreary "before" and the more bracing "after." And "Shall We Dance?" -- in both its original Japanese and Hollywood versions -- provided a much better renewal-through-dance-lessons fable.

Also, there's a surprising (but rather sour) twist at the end that some may find less than satisfying. There are some pleasurable elements to be sure, but -- title notwithstanding -- charm is in short supply.

The film contains a few rough and crude words and expressions, a nongraphic premarital sexual encounter, fleeting sexual banter, a car wreck and a bloody victim, a suicide theme, and the dispersal of cremated remains. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
